primary_meaning: God’s life-giving gift—especially the Holy Spirit—imparting spiritual renewal, salvation, and eternal life.
primary_basis: John 7:37–39 explicitly identifies the promised rivers of living water with the Holy Spirit.
John 4:10–14 portrays Jesus’ living water as an inward, enduring gift that springs up to eternal life.
Isaiah 44:3 links poured-out water with the outpouring of God’s Spirit and blessing.
Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8 depict life-giving waters flowing from God’s eschatological presence.
Revelation 21:6; 22:1–2, 17 associates the water of life with God’s free gift, healing, and eternal life.

alternatives.meaning: God himself as the inexhaustible source or fountain of life, contrasted with false gods and human substitutes.
basis: Jeremiah 2:13 calls the LORD “the fountain of living waters.”
Jeremiah 17:13 similarly identifies the LORD as the fountain of living water.

alternatives.meaning: Jesus Christ or the salvation and revelation he personally gives, rather than the Holy Spirit considered separately.
basis: John 4:10–14 centers the gift on Jesus and his ability to give eternal life.
John 6:35 and Revelation 21:6 are often read alongside the living-water sayings as invitations to receive life through Christ.

alternatives.meaning: Eschatological life, healing, and restoration flowing from God’s presence in the renewed creation.
basis: Ezekiel 47:1–12 describes temple water bringing life and healing wherever it flows.
Zechariah 14:8 places living waters in the final reign of the LORD.
Revelation 22:1–2 presents the river of the water of life in the New Jerusalem.
John 3:5 is sometimes connected with John’s water imagery.
Early Christian and sacramental interpretation often associates John 4 and John 7 with baptism and the gift of the Spirit.

alternatives.meaning: Literal fresh, flowing, or spring water, without an inherent symbolic referent.
basis: Genesis 26:19 uses the expression for fresh spring water.
Leviticus 14:5–6 and Numbers 19:17 use “living water” in purification rites to mean running or fresh water.
Song of Songs 4:15 uses it poetically for flowing water.

notes: There is broad Christian consensus that, when used symbolically in the New Testament, “living water” signifies God’s life-giving saving gift, with the Holy Spirit as the clearest specific referent because of John 7:39. The imagery remains context-sensitive: some passages emphasize God as the source, Christ as giver, eternal life, or eschatological restoration rather than distinguishing these sharply.
